statement: Learner multiplies the degree of financial leverage by (1 - tax rate), treating DFL as a post-tax quantity. Tax scales EPS and EBT by the same factor, so it cancels out of a ratio of percentage changes and never enters DFL.
ladder: Before the number - which two quantities is financial leverage comparing?
Hold the tax rate fixed and move EBIT by 10%. Does the percentage change in EPS depend on that rate at all?
Tax multiplies both EPS and EBT by the same factor. What happens to a constant that appears in both halves of a ratio?
Work it as EBIT divided by (EBIT minus interest). The tax rate is not in that expression, and it never was.

statement: Learner computes Contribution / EBIT when asked for financial leverage, or EBIT / EBT when asked for operating leverage. The two degrees are confused because both are ratios built from EBIT.
ladder: Which risk is this question asking about - the cost structure above EBIT, or the financing below it?
Operating leverage looks upward, to contribution and fixed costs. Financial leverage looks downward, to interest. Which way does this one look?
Financial leverage is EBIT over EBT. Operating leverage is contribution over EBIT.
Check which figure you put on top. If interest appears anywhere in your working, you are computing financial leverage.

statement: Learner subtracts interest from the numerator as well as the denominator, computing (EBIT - Interest) / (EBIT - Interest) style expressions, or nets interest out of EBIT before forming the ratio.
ladder: What does the numerator of this ratio represent, before any interest is paid?
You subtracted interest twice. Where should it appear - the top, the bottom, or both?
EBIT is the top line here, untouched. Interest comes off once, in the denominator.
A ratio whose numerator and denominator are the same expression is always 1.00, whatever the figures. That is the signal you subtracted twice.
